text: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{1+x}\) for \(x>-1\). Let \(g(x)=e^{mx},\ m\in\mathbb Q\), and \(h(x)=f(x)g(x)\). The coefficient of \(x^2\) in the Maclaurin series for \(h(x)\) is \(\dfrac74\).

stem_blocks.text: Let \(f(x)=\sqrt{1+x}\) for \(x>-1\).
Let \(g(x)=e^{mx},\ m\in\mathbb Q\). Consider the function \(h\) defined by \(h(x)=f(x)\times g(x)\) for \(x>-1\).
It is given that the \(x^2\) term in the Maclaurin series for \(h(x)\) has a coefficient of \(\dfrac74\).

blocks.text: Show that \(f''(x)=-\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{(1+x)^3}}\).
Use mathematical induction to prove that \(f^{(n)}(x)=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{n-1}\dfrac{(2n-3)!}{(n-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-n}\), for \(n\in\mathbb Z,\ n\ge2\).
Find the possible values of \(m\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(f''(x)=-\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{(1+x)^3}}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Use mathematical induction to prove the stated formula for \(f^{(n)}(x)\), for \(n\in\mathbb Z,\ n\ge2\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Find the possible values of \(m\).

answers.text: The stated formula holds for all \(n\in\mathbb Z,\ n\ge2\), by mathematical induction.

solution.outline: The complete official answers and all three complete official methods for part (c) below are the scoring authority for this question.

rows.text:
attempt to use the chain rule M1
\(f'(x)=\dfrac12(1+x)^{-\frac12}\) A1
\(f''(x)=-\dfrac14(1+x)^{-\frac32}=-\dfrac{1}{4\sqrt{(1+x)^3}}\) A1 AG
Note: Award M1A0A0 for \(f'(x)=\dfrac1{\sqrt{1+x}}\) or equivalent seen.
[3 marks]

mark_points.description: attempt to use the chain rule

rows.text:
let \(n=2\)
\(f''(x)=-\dfrac1{4\sqrt{(1+x)^3}}=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^1\dfrac{1!}{0!}(1+x)^{\frac12-2}\) R1
Note: Award R0 for not starting at \(n=2\). Award subsequent marks as appropriate.
assume true for \(n=k\), so \(f^{(k)}(x)=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}\dfrac{(2k-3)!}{(k-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k}\) M1
Note: Do not award M1 for statements such as “let \(n=k\)” or “\(n=k\) is true”. Subsequent marks can still be awarded.
consider \(n=k+1\)
\(\mathrm{LHS}=f^{(k+1)}(x)=\dfrac{d(f^{(k)}(x))}{dx}\) M1
\(=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}\dfrac{(2k-3)!}{(k-2)!}\left(\dfrac12-k\right)(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\) (or equivalent) A1
EITHER
\(\mathrm{RHS}=f^{(k+1)}(x)=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^k\dfrac{(2k-1)!}{(k-1)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\) (or equivalent) A1
\(=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^k\dfrac{(2k-1)(2k-2)(2k-3)!}{(k-1)(k-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\) A1
Note: Award A1 for \(\dfrac{(2k-1)!}{(k-1)!}=\dfrac{(2k-1)(2k-2)(2k-3)!}{(k-1)(k-2)!}=\dfrac{2(2k-1)(2k-3)!}{(k-2)!}\).
\(=\left(-\dfrac14\right)\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}\dfrac{(2k-1)(2k-2)(2k-3)!}{(k-1)(k-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\) A1
\(=\left(-\dfrac12\right)\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}\dfrac{(2k-1)(2k-3)!}{(k-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\)
Note: Award A1 for leading coefficient of \(-\dfrac14\).
\(=\left(\dfrac12-k\right)\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}\dfrac{(2k-3)!}{(k-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\) A1
OR
Note: The following A marks can be awarded in any order.
\(=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}\dfrac{(2k-3)!}{(k-2)!}\left(\dfrac{1-2k}{2}\right)(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\)
\(=\left(-\dfrac12\right)\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}\dfrac{(2k-1)(2k-3)!}{(k-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\) A1
Note: Award A1 for isolating \(2k-1\) correctly.
\(=\left(-\dfrac12\right)\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{k-1}\dfrac{(2k-1)!}{(2k-2)(k-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\) A1
Note: Award A1 for multiplying top and bottom by \(k-1\) or \(2(k-1)\).
\(=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^k\dfrac{(2k-1)!}{(k-1)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-k-1}\) A1
\(=\left(-\dfrac14\right)^{(k+1)-1}\dfrac{(2(k+1)-3)!}{((k+1)-2)!}(1+x)^{\frac12-(k+1)}=\mathrm{RHS}\)
THEN
since true for \(n=2\), and true for \(n=k+1\) if true for \(n=k\), the statement is true for all \(n\in\mathbb Z,n\ge2\) by mathematical induction R1
Note: To obtain the final R1, at least four of the previous marks must have been awarded.
[9 marks]

coefficient of \(x^2\) is \(\dfrac{m^2}{2}+\dfrac m2-\dfrac18\) A1

\(=1\times m^2+2m\times\dfrac12+1\times\left(-\dfrac14\right)(=m^2+m-\dfrac14)\) A1
\(4m^2+4m-15=0\)
\((2m+5)(2m-3)=0\) A1

text: (a) Prove by mathematical induction that dⁿ/dxⁿ(x²eˣ) = [x² + 2nx + n(n − 1)]eˣ for n ∈ ℤ⁺. (b) Hence or otherwise, determine the Maclaurin series of f(x) = x²eˣ in ascending powers of x, up to and including the term in x⁴. (c) Hence or otherwise, determine the value of limₓ→₀ [(x²eˣ − x²)³/x⁹].

answers.text: For n = 1, both sides equal eˣ(x² + 2x). Assuming the result for n = k and differentiating gives [x² + 2(k + 1)x + k(k + 1)]eˣ, so the result is true for all n ∈ ℤ⁺.

solution.outline: The complete official answers and official marking detail below are the scoring authority for this question.

rows.text:
For n = 1

LHS: d/dx(x²eˣ) = x²eˣ + 2xeˣ (= eˣ(x² + 2x))  A1

RHS: (x² + 2(1)x + 1(1 − 1))eˣ (= eˣ(x² + 2x))  A1

so true for n = 1

now assume true for n = k; i.e. dᵏ/dxᵏ(x²eˣ) = [x² + 2kx + k(k − 1)]eˣ  M1

Note: Do not award M1 for statements such as “let n = k”. Subsequent marks can still be awarded.

attempt to differentiate the RHS  M1

dᵏ⁺¹/dxᵏ⁺¹(x²eˣ) = d/dx{[x² + 2kx + k(k − 1)]eˣ}

= (2x + 2k)eˣ + (x² + 2kx + k(k − 1))eˣ  A1

= [x² + 2(k + 1)x + k(k + 1)]eˣ  A1

so true for n = k implies true for n = k + 1

therefore n = 1 true and n = k true ⇒ n = k + 1 true

therefore, true for all n ∈ ℤ⁺  R1

Note: Award R1 only if three of the previous four marks have been awarded.

[7 marks]

classification_review.solving_path: Substitutes omega1 and reduces (omega1-1)^3 to (e^(i pi/6))^3. Uses exponential or trigonometric form to obtain i. Writes i with its full family of arguments before taking cube roots. Divides the arguments by three and applies the translation z=1+(z-1). Obtains omega2=1+e^(i5pi/6). Obtains omega3=1+e^(i9pi/6), equivalently 1-i. Converts the three roots to Cartesian coordinates or correctly translates their unit-circle positions. Plots A at (1+sqrt(3)/2,1/2). Plots B at (1-sqrt(3)/2,1/2). Plots C at (1,-1). Forms the complex difference omega1-omega3 or the coordinate displacement AC. Computes the modulus sqrt(3/4+9/4). Obtains AC=sqrt(3). Divides by z^3 to obtain ((z-1)/z)^3=i and applies de Moivre's theorem. Obtains (alpha-1)/alpha=e^(i pi/6), or the equivalent reciprocal form. Rearranges to alpha=1/(1-e^(i pi/6)). Writes e^(i pi/6) in Cartesian form. Obtains a correct Cartesian denominator, such as 2-sqrt(3)-i after scaling. Uses the complex conjugate to rationalize the denominator. Forms the correct conjugate-product numerator. Simplifies the real component of alpha correctly. Obtains Re(alpha)=1/2.

text: Consider integers a and b such that a^2+b^2 is exactly divisible by 4. Prove by contradiction that a and b cannot both be odd.

stem_blocks.text: Consider integers \(a\) and \(b\) such that \(a^2+b^2\) is exactly divisible by 4.

blocks.text: Prove by contradiction that \(a\) and \(b\) cannot both be odd.

parts.label: main
parts.text: Prove by contradiction that \(a\) and \(b\) cannot both be odd.

answers.text: Assuming both integers are odd leads to \(a^2+b^2=4(m^2+m+n^2+n)+2\), so \(a^2+b^2\) is not divisible by 4. This contradicts the premise; hence \(a\) and \(b\) cannot both be odd.

solution.outline: The complete official answers and official markscheme below are the scoring authority for this question.

rows.text:
Assume that \(a\) and \(b\) are both odd. \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

Note: Award \(\mathrm{M0}\) for statements such as "let \(a\) and \(b\) be both odd".

Note: Subsequent marks after this \(\mathrm{M1}\) are independent of this mark and can be awarded.

Then \(a=2m+1\) and \(b=2n+1\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(a^2+b^2=(2m+1)^2+(2n+1)^2\)

\(=4m^2+4m+1+4n^2+4n+1\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(=4(m^2+m+n^2+n)+2\) \(\quad\mathrm{(A1)}\)

\(4(m^2+m+n^2+n)\) is always divisible by 4 but 2 is not divisible by 4. (or equivalent) \(\quad\mathrm{R1}\)

\(\Rightarrow a^2+b^2\) is not divisible by 4, a contradiction. (or equivalent) \(\quad\mathrm{R1}\)

hence \(a\) and \(b\) cannot both be odd. \(\quad\mathrm{AG}\)

Note: Award a maximum of \(\mathrm{M1A0A0(A0)R1R1}\) for considering identical or two consecutive odd numbers for \(a\) and \(b\).

[6 marks]

text: Consider the three planes Pi_1: 2x-y+z=4, Pi_2: x-2y+3z=5 and Pi_3: -9x+3y-2z=32. Show the intersection result, find the line of intersection of Pi_1 and Pi_2, and find the distance between that line and Pi_3.

solution.outline: The complete official answers and official markscheme below are the scoring authority for this question.

rows.text:
METHOD 1

attempt to eliminate a variable \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

obtain a pair of equations in two variables

EITHER
\(-3x+z=-3\) and \(-3x+z=44\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1,A1}\)

OR
\(-5x+y=-7\) and \(-5x+y=40\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1,A1}\)

OR
\(3x-z=3\) and \(3x-z=-\dfrac{79}{5}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1,A1}\)

THEN

the two lines are parallel, since the constants are inconsistent \(\quad\mathrm{R1}\)

Note: There are other possible pairs of equations in two variables. To obtain the final \(\mathrm{R1}\), at least the initial \(\mathrm{M1}\) must have been awarded.

hence the three planes do not intersect \(\quad\mathrm{AG}\)

[4 marks]

METHOD 2

vector product of the two normals is \(\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-5\\-3\end{pmatrix}\), or equivalent \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}\), or equivalent \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

Note: Award \(\mathrm{A0}\) if \(\mathbf r=\) is missing. Subsequent marks may still be awarded.

Attempt to substitute \((1+\lambda,-2+5\lambda,3\lambda)\) in \(\Pi_3\) \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(-9(1+\lambda)+3(-2+5\lambda)-2(3\lambda)=32\)

\(-15=32\), a contradiction \(\quad\mathrm{R1}\)

hence the three planes do not intersect \(\quad\mathrm{AG}\)

[4 marks]

METHOD 3

attempt to eliminate a variable \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(-3y+5z=6\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(-3y+5z=100\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(0=94\), a contradiction \(\quad\mathrm{R1}\)

Note: Accept other equivalent alternatives. Accept other valid methods. To obtain the final \(\mathrm{R1}\), at least the initial \(\mathrm{M1}\) must have been awarded.

hence the three planes do not intersect \(\quad\mathrm{AG}\)

[4 marks]

mark_points.description: Attempts to eliminate a variable, or begins an equivalent valid method such as a vector-line substitution route.
Obtains the first correct equation or vector component needed for an official method.
Obtains the second correct equation or vector line needed for an official method.
Shows the inconsistency or contradiction and concludes that the three planes do not intersect.
Verifies that \(P(1,-2,0)\) satisfies both \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

rows.text:
METHOD 1

attempt to find the vector product of the two normals \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(\begin{pmatrix}2\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}\times\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\3\end{pmatrix}\)

\(=\begin{pmatrix}-1\\-5\\-3\end{pmatrix}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1,A1}\)

Note: Award \(\mathrm{A1A0}\) if \(\mathbf r=\) is missing. Accept any multiple of the direction vector. Working for (b)(ii) may be seen in part (a) Method 2. In this case penalize lack of \(\mathbf r=\) only once.

METHOD 2

attempt to eliminate a variable from \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\) \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(3x-z=3\) OR \(3y-5z=-6\) OR \(5x-y=7\)

Let \(x=t\). Substituting \(x=t\) in \(3x-z=3\) gives \(z=-3+3t\) and \(y=5t-7\), for all three variables in parametric form \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(\mathbf r=\begin{pmatrix}0\\-7\\-3\end{pmatrix}+\lambda\begin{pmatrix}1\\5\\3\end{pmatrix}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1,A1}\)

Note: Award \(\mathrm{A1A0}\) if \(\mathbf r=\) is missing. Accept any multiple of the direction vector. Accept other position vectors which satisfy both the planes \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).

[5 marks]

mark_points.description: Attempts to find the vector product of the two normals, or eliminates a variable from \(\Pi_1\) and \(\Pi_2\).
Obtains a correct direction vector, or obtains a valid parametric relationship for the line.
Uses a valid point or position vector on the line of intersection.
Gives a complete valid vector equation of the line of intersection.

rows.text:
METHOD 1

the line connecting \(L\) and \(\Pi_3\) is given by \(L_1\)

attempt to substitute position and direction vector to form \(L_1\) \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(\mathbf s=\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+t\begin{pmatrix}-9\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

substitute \((1-9t,-2+3t,-2t)\) in \(\Pi_3\) \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(-9(1-9t)+3(-2+3t)-2(-2t)=32\)

\(94t=47\Rightarrow t=\dfrac12\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

attempt to find distance between \((1,-2,0)\) and their point \(\left(-\dfrac72,-\dfrac12,-1\right)\) \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(\left|\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}+\dfrac12\begin{pmatrix}-9\\3\\-2\end{pmatrix}-\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}\right|=\dfrac12\sqrt{(-9)^2+3^2+(-2)^2}\)

\(=\dfrac{\sqrt{94}}{2}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

[6 marks]

METHOD 2

unit normal vector equation of \(\Pi_3\) is given by \(\dfrac{\begin{pmatrix}-9\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}}{\sqrt{81+9+4}}=\dfrac{32}{\sqrt{94}}\) \(\quad\mathrm{(M1),A1}\)

let \(\Pi_4\) be the plane parallel to \(\Pi_3\) and passing through \(P\), then the normal vector equation of \(\Pi_4\) is given by \(\begin{pmatrix}-9\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-9\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\\0\end{pmatrix}=-15\) \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

unit normal vector equation of \(\Pi_4\) is given by \(\dfrac{\begin{pmatrix}-9\\3\\2\end{pmatrix}\cdot\begin{pmatrix}x\\y\\z\end{pmatrix}}{\sqrt{81+9+4}}=\dfrac{-15}{\sqrt{94}}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

distance between the planes is \(\dfrac{32}{\sqrt{94}}-\dfrac{-15}{\sqrt{94}}\) \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(=\dfrac{47}{\sqrt{94}}=\dfrac{\sqrt{94}}{2}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

[6 marks]

Total [15 marks]

text: The function f is defined by f(x)=e^x sin x, and the function g is defined by g(x)=e^x cos x. Work with Maclaurin series, derivatives, an approximate integral and a limit.

stem_blocks.text: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=e^x\sin x\), where \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).
The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=e^x\cos x\), where \(x\in\mathbb{R}\).

blocks.text: Find the Maclaurin series for \(f(x)\) up to and including the \(x^3\) term.
Hence, find an approximate value for \(\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\sin(x^2)\,dx\).
Show that \(g(x)\) satisfies the equation \(g''(x)=2(g'(x)-g(x))\).
Hence, deduce that \(g^{(4)}(x)=2(g'''(x)-g''(x))\).
Using the result from part (c), find the Maclaurin series for \(g(x)\) up to and including the \(x^4\) term.
Hence, or otherwise, determine the value of \(\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{e^x\cos x-1-x}{x^3}\).

solution.outline: The complete official answers and official markscheme below are the scoring authority for this question.

rows.text:
METHOD 1

recognition of both known series \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(e^x=1+\dfrac{x}{1!}+\dfrac{x^2}{2!}+\cdots\) and \(\sin x=x-\dfrac{x^3}{3!}+\dfrac{x^5}{5!}+\cdots\)

attempt to multiply the two series up to and including \(x^3\) term \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(e^x\sin x=\left(1+\dfrac{x}{1!}+\dfrac{x^2}{2!}+\cdots\right)\left(x-\dfrac{x^3}{3!}+\dfrac{x^5}{5!}+\cdots\right)\)

\(=x-\dfrac{x^3}{3!}+x^2+\dfrac{x^3}{2!}+\cdots\) \(\quad\mathrm{(A1)}\)

\(e^x\sin x=x+x^2+\dfrac13x^3+\cdots\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

[4 marks]

METHOD 2

\(f(x)=e^x\sin x\)

\(f'(x)=e^x\cos x+e^x\sin x\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(f''(x)=e^x\cos x-e^x\sin x+e^x\sin x+e^x\cos x(=2e^x\cos x)\)

\(f'''(x)=2e^x\cos x-2e^x\sin x\)

\(f''(x)=2e^x\cos x\) and \(f'''(x)=2e^x(\cos x-\sin x)\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

substitute \(x=0\) into \(f\) or its derivatives to obtain Maclaurin series \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(e^x\sin x=0+\dfrac{x}{1!}\times1+\dfrac{x^2}{2!}\times2+\dfrac{x^3}{3!}\times2+\cdots\)

\(e^x\sin x=x+x^2+\dfrac13x^3+\cdots\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

[4 marks]

mark_points.description: Recognizes both known series, or starts the derivative-based Maclaurin route.
Attempts to multiply the series up to and including the \(x^3\) term, or obtains the needed first derivative value route.
Obtains the intermediate \(x-x^3/3!+x^2+x^3/2!+\cdots\), or the corresponding derivative values.
Obtains \(e^x\sin x=x+x^2+\dfrac13x^3+\cdots\).

rows.text:
\(e^{x^2}\sin(x^2)=x^2+x^4+\dfrac13x^6+\cdots\) \(\quad\mathrm{(A1)}\)

substituting their expression and attempt to integrate \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(\displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{x^2}\sin(x^2)\,dx\approx\int_0^1\left(x^2+x^4+\dfrac13x^6\right)dx\)

Note: Condone absence of limits up to this stage.

\(=\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{x^5}{5}+\dfrac{x^7}{21}\right]_0^1\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(=\dfrac{61}{105}\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

[4 marks]

mark_points.description: Substitutes \(x^2\) into the series to obtain \(e^{x^2}\sin(x^2)=x^2+x^4+\dfrac13x^6+\cdots\).
Substitutes the series expression into the integral and attempts to integrate.
Obtains \(\left[\dfrac{x^3}{3}+\dfrac{x^5}{5}+\dfrac{x^7}{21}\right]_0^1\).
Obtains \(\dfrac{61}{105}\).

rows.text:
attempt to use product rule at least once \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(g'(x)=e^x\cos x-e^x\sin x\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(g''(x)=e^x\cos x-e^x\sin x-e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x(=-2e^x\sin x)\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

EITHER

\(2(g'(x)-g(x))=2(e^x\cos x-e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x)=-2e^x\sin x\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

OR

\(g''(x)=2(e^x\cos x-e^x\sin x-e^x\cos x)\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

THEN

\(g''(x)=2(g'(x)-g(x))\) \(\quad\mathrm{AG}\)

Note: Accept working with each side separately to obtain \(-2e^x\sin x\).

mark_points.description: Attempts to use the product rule at least once.
Obtains \(g'(x)=e^x\cos x-e^x\sin x\).
Obtains \(g''(x)=-2e^x\sin x\).
Shows that \(2(g'(x)-g(x))\) gives the same expression as \(g''(x)\).

rows.text:
\(g'''(x)=2(g''(x)-g'(x))\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(g^{(4)}(x)=2(g'''(x)-g''(x))\) \(\quad\mathrm{AG}\)

Note: Accept working with each side separately to obtain \(-4e^x\cos x\).

[5 marks]

mark_points.description: Deduces \(g^{(4)}(x)=2(g'''(x)-g''(x))\), for example by first differentiating to \(g'''(x)=2(g''(x)-g'(x))\).

rows.text:
attempt to substitute \(x=0\) into a derivative \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(g(0)=1\), \(g'(0)=1\), \(g''(0)=0\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(g'''(0)=-2\), \(g^{(4)}(0)=-4\) \(\quad\mathrm{(A1)}\)

attempt to substitute into Maclaurin formula \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(g(x)=1+x-\dfrac{2}{3!}x^3-\dfrac{4}{4!}x^4+\cdots\left(=1+x-\dfrac13x^3-\dfrac16x^4+\cdots\right)\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

Note: Do not award any marks for approaches that do not use the part (c) result.

[5 marks]

mark_points.description: Attempts to substitute \(x=0\) into a derivative using the part (c) result.
Attempts to substitute the derivative values into the Maclaurin formula.
Obtains \(g(x)=1+x-\dfrac13x^3-\dfrac16x^4+\cdots\).

rows.text:
METHOD 1

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{e^x\cos x-1-x}{x^3}=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{\left(1+x-\dfrac13x^3-\dfrac16x^4+\cdots\right)-1-x}{x^3}\) \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(=\lim_{x\to0}\left(-\dfrac13-\dfrac16x+\cdots\right)\) \(\quad\mathrm{(A1)}\)

\(=-\dfrac13\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

Note: Condone the omission of \(+\cdots\) in their working.

METHOD 2

\(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{e^x\cos x-1-x}{x^3}=\dfrac00\) indeterminate form, attempt to apply L'Hopital's rule \(\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

\(=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{e^x\cos x-e^x\sin x-1}{3x^2}\left(=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{g'(x)-1}{3x^2}\right)\)

\(=\dfrac00\), using L'Hopital's rule again

\(=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{-2e^x\sin x}{6x}\left(=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{g''(x)}{6x}\right)\)

\(=\dfrac00\), using L'Hopital's rule again

\(=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{-2e^x\sin x-2e^x\cos x}{6}\left(=\lim_{x\to0}\dfrac{g'''(x)}{6}\right)\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

\(=-\dfrac13\) \(\quad\mathrm{A1}\)

[3 marks]

Total [21 marks]

Nicky plays a game with this four-sided die. She is allowed a maximum of five rolls. Her score is the sum of the results of each roll, and she wins if her score is at least 10. After three rolls she has a score of 4.

David has two pairs of unbiased four-sided dice, a yellow pair and a red pair. Both yellow dice have faces labelled 1, 2, 3 and 4. Let S represent the sum obtained by rolling the two yellow dice; the probability distribution for S is shown in the question.

The first red die has faces labelled 1, 2, 2 and 3. The second red die has faces labelled 1, a, a and b, where a<b and a and b are positive integers. The red-pair sum distribution is the same as the yellow-pair sum distribution.

After three rolls the score is 4, so the last two rolls must total 6, 7 or 8. P(T=6)=2(0.3)(0.1)+(0.2)^2=0.10, P(T=7)=2(0.2)(0.1)=0.04 and P(T=8)=(0.1)^2=0.01. The required probability is 0.15.
The largest yellow sum is 8 and the largest red sum is 3+b, so 3+b=8 and b=5.

The matching distribution requires the red pair to have four outcomes with sum 5, matching P(S=5)=4/16 for the yellow pair. Since the first red die has two faces labelled 2 and the second red die has two faces labelled a, the four repeated outcomes have sum a+2. Hence a+2=5 and a=3.

text: A complex-number geometry question using an Argand diagram. Points Z1, O and Z2 form triangle Z1OZ2, with z1=r1 e^(i alpha) and z2=r2 e^(i theta). Students use conjugates and arguments to identify a right angle, handle the equilateral case, prove z1^2+z2^2=z1z2, connect the roots of z^2+az+b=0 to a^2-3b=0, and determine which value of a gives the unique permitted equilateral triangle for z^2+az+12=0.

stem_blocks.text: In the Argand diagram, points Z1, O and Z2 are the vertices of triangle Z1OZ2 described anticlockwise.
The point Z1 represents z1=r1 e^(i alpha), where r1>0. The point Z2 represents z2=r2 e^(i theta), where r2>0.
Angles alpha and theta are measured anticlockwise from the positive direction of the real axis such that 0<=alpha,theta<2*pi and 0<alpha-theta<pi.
In parts (c), (d) and (e), consider the case where Z1OZ2 is an equilateral triangle.
Let z1 and z2 be the distinct roots of z^2+az+b=0, where z is complex and a,b are real. Then consider z^2+az+12=0, where z is complex and a is real.

blocks.text: Show that z1 z2* = r1 r2 e^(i(alpha-theta)), where z2* is the complex conjugate of z2.
Given that Re(z1 z2*)=0, show that Z1OZ2 is a right-angled triangle.
In the equilateral case, express z1 in terms of z2.
Hence show that z1^2+z2^2=z1z2.
Use the result from part (c)(ii) to show that a^2-3b=0.
Given that 0<alpha-theta<pi, deduce that only one equilateral triangle Z1OZ2 can be formed from the point O and the roots of z^2+az+12=0.

parts.label: e

answers.text: Since z2*=r2 e^(-i theta), z1 z2*=r1 e^(i alpha) r2 e^(-i theta)=r1 r2 e^(i(alpha-theta)).
Re(z1 z2*)=r1 r2 cos(alpha-theta). If this is zero, then cos(alpha-theta)=0 because r1,r2>0. Since 0<alpha-theta<pi, alpha-theta=pi/2, so the angle at O is a right angle and Z1OZ2 is right-angled.
In an equilateral triangle r1=r2 and alpha-theta=pi/3. Hence z1/z2=e^(i*pi/3), so z1=z2 e^(i*pi/3). Equivalently, z1=z2(cos(pi/3)+i sin(pi/3))=z2(1/2+sqrt(3)i/2).
Substituting z1=z2 e^(i*pi/3) gives z1^2+z2^2=z2^2 e^(2i*pi/3)+z2^2=z2^2(e^(2i*pi/3)+1). Since e^(2i*pi/3)+1=e^(i*pi/3), this becomes z2^2 e^(i*pi/3)=z2(z2 e^(i*pi/3))=z1z2.
By the sum and product of roots, z1+z2=-a and z1z2=b. Then a^2=(z1+z2)^2=z1^2+z2^2+2z1z2=z1z2+2z1z2=3z1z2=3b, so a^2-3b=0.

With b=12, a^2-3*12=0, so a=+-6. If a=-6, the roots are 3+-sqrt(3)i and the corresponding argument difference is -5pi/3, which does not satisfy 0<alpha-theta<pi. If a=6, the roots are -3+-sqrt(3)i and alpha-theta=pi/3, which does satisfy the condition. Hence only one equilateral triangle can be formed.

text: A house-plan diagram shows a narrow passageway of width 3/4 m perpendicular to a room of width 6 m. Points A, C and B are collinear around the corner, L is the length AB, and alpha is the angle AB makes with the room wall where 0<alpha<pi/2. Students derive L=(3/4)sec(alpha)+6cosec(alpha), differentiate to find the stationary angle alpha=arctan(2), use the second derivative to justify a minimum, find the minimum length, and decide whether an 11.25 m horizontal pole can be carried from the passageway into the room.

stem_blocks.text: A diagram shows the plan of part of a house. A narrow passageway with width 3/4 m is perpendicular to a room of width 6 m. There is a corner at point C. Points A and B are variable points on the base of the walls such that A, C and B lie on a straight line.
Let L denote the length AB in metres. Let alpha be the angle that AB makes with the room wall, where 0<alpha<pi/2.
Two people need to carry a pole of length 11.25 m from the passageway into the room. It must be carried horizontally.

blocks.text: Show that L=(3/4)sec(alpha)+6cosec(alpha).
(i) Find dL/dalpha. (ii) When dL/dalpha=0, show that alpha=arctan(2).
(i) Find d2L/dalpha2. (ii) When alpha=arctan(2), show that d2L/dalpha2=(45/4)sqrt(5).
(i) Hence, justify that L is a minimum when alpha=arctan(2). (ii) Determine this minimum value of L.
Determine whether carrying the 11.25 m pole horizontally from the passageway into the room is possible, giving a reason for your answer.

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that L=(3/4)sec(alpha)+6cosec(alpha).

parts.label: b
parts.text: (i) Find dL/dalpha. (ii) When dL/dalpha=0, show that alpha=arctan(2).

parts.label: c
parts.text: (i) Find d2L/dalpha2. (ii) When alpha=arctan(2), show that d2L/dalpha2=(45/4)sqrt(5).

parts.label: d
parts.text: (i) Hence, justify that L is a minimum when alpha=arctan(2). (ii) Determine this minimum value of L.

parts.label: e

answers.text: Using the two right triangles, AC=(3/4)sec(alpha) and CB=6cosec(alpha), so L=AC+CB=(3/4)sec(alpha)+6cosec(alpha).
dL/dalpha=(3/4)sec(alpha)tan(alpha)-6cosec(alpha)cot(alpha). Setting this equal to zero gives (3/4)tan^3(alpha)-6=0, so tan(alpha)=2 and alpha=arctan(2).

d2L/dalpha2=(3/4)sec(alpha)tan^2(alpha)+(3/4)sec^3(alpha)+6cosec(alpha)cot^2(alpha)+6cosec^3(alpha). At alpha=arctan(2), sec(alpha)=sqrt(5), cosec(alpha)=sqrt(5)/2 and cot(alpha)=1/2, giving d2L/dalpha2=(45/4)sqrt(5).
Since d2L/dalpha2>0 at the stationary point, L is a minimum when alpha=arctan(2). The minimum value is Lmin=(3/4)sqrt(5)+6(sqrt(5)/2)=15sqrt(5)/4.

parts.label: main
parts.text: Use mathematical induction to prove that \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{r}{(r+1)!}=1-\frac{1}{(n+1)!}\) for all integers \(n\ge 1\).

answers.text: The statement is true for \(n=1\). Assuming it is true for \(n=k\), adding the \((k+1)\)th term gives \(1-\frac{1}{(k+2)!}\), so the statement is true for \(n=k+1\). Therefore it is true for all integers \(n\ge 1\).

solution.outline: Verify the base case, state the induction assumption, add the \((k+1)\)th term, simplify the factorial expression to the required \(P(k+1)\) form, then make the induction conclusion.

rows.text: Let \(P(n)\) be the proposition that \(\sum_{r=1}^{n}\frac{r}{(r+1)!}=1-\frac{1}{(n+1)!}\) for all integers \(n\ge 1\). Considering \(P(1)\), LHS \(=\frac12\) and RHS \(=\frac12\), so \(P(1)\) is true. Assume \(P(k)\) is true, that is \(\sum_{r=1}^{k}\frac{r}{(r+1)!}=1-\frac{1}{(k+1)!}\). Note: do not award the assumption mark for statements such as 'let \(n=k\)' or '\(n=k\) is true'; later marks are independent. Considering \(P(k+1)\), \(\sum_{r=1}^{k+1}\frac{r}{(r+1)!}=\sum_{r=1}^{k}\frac{r}{(r+1)!}+\frac{k+1}{((k+1)+1)!}\). This becomes \(1-\frac{1}{(k+1)!}+\frac{k+1}{(k+2)!}=1-\frac{(k+2)-(k+1)}{(k+2)!}=1-\frac{1}{(k+2)!}=1-\frac{1}{((k+1)+1)!}\). Thus \(P(k+1)\) is true whenever \(P(k)\) is true and \(P(1)\) is true, so \(P(n)\) is true for all integers \(n\ge 1\). Note: to obtain the final reasoning mark, any four of the previous marks must have been awarded.

text: A circle with equation x^2 + y^2 = 9 has centre (0, 0) and radius 3. A triangle PQR is inscribed in the circle with vertices P(-3, 0), Q(x, y), and R(x, -y), where Q and R are variable points in the first and fourth quadrants respectively. Show y = sqrt(9 - x^2), form the area of triangle PQR, differentiate it, and find the y-coordinate of R when the area is maximum.

stem_blocks.text: A circle with equation \(x^2+y^2=9\) has centre \((0,0)\) and radius \(3\).
A triangle, \(PQR\), is inscribed in the circle with vertices at \(P(-3,0)\), \(Q(x,y)\) and \(R(x,-y)\), where \(Q\) and \(R\) are variable points in the first and fourth quadrants respectively.

stem_blocks.alt: Circle x squared plus y squared equals 9 with shaded triangle PQR, P at (-3, 0), Q at (x, y), and R at (x, -y).
stem_blocks.caption: Diagram of triangle PQR inscribed in the circle.

blocks.text: For point Q, show that \(y=\sqrt{9-x^2}\).
Hence, find an expression for \(A\), the area of triangle \(PQR\), in terms of \(x\).
Show that \(\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\dfrac{9-3x-2x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\).
Hence or otherwise, find the \(y\)-coordinate of \(R\) such that \(A\) is a maximum.

answers.text: \({y=\sqrt{9-x^2}}\), since \(Q\) is in the first quadrant.

solution.outline: Use circle geometry to express y in terms of x, form the triangle area, differentiate the area function, and solve the stationary condition for the valid point.

rows.text: From \(x^2+y^2=9\), \(y=\pm\sqrt{9-x^2}\). Since \(Q\) is in the first quadrant, \(y=\sqrt{9-x^2}\).

mark_points.description: Derives \(y=\sqrt{9-x^2}\), using the positive root for point \(Q\).

rows.text: The base \(QR=2y=2\sqrt{9-x^2}\), and the perpendicular height from \(P\) to \(QR\) is \(x+3\). Therefore \(A=\frac12(2\sqrt{9-x^2})(x+3)=(x+3)\sqrt{9-x^2}\).

mark_points.description: Identifies a correct base expression, for example \(QR=2y=2\sqrt{9-x^2}\).
Uses \(A=\frac12bh\) with base \(QR\) and height \(x+3\).
Obtains \(A=(x+3)\sqrt{9-x^2}\).

rows.text: Differentiate \(A=(x+3)(9-x^2)^{1/2}\) using the product rule and chain rule. \(\dfrac{dA}{dx}=\sqrt{9-x^2}-(x+3)\dfrac{x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}=\dfrac{9-x^2-x^2-3x}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}=\dfrac{9-3x-2x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\).

Uses the chain rule to differentiate \(\sqrt{9-x^2}\).
Obtains an equivalent unsimplified derivative, such as \(\sqrt{9-x^2}-\dfrac{x(x+3)}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\).
Simplifies to \(\dfrac{9-3x-2x^2}{\sqrt{9-x^2}}\).

rows.text: For a maximum, solve \(\dfrac{dA}{dx}=0\), so \(9-3x-2x^2=0\). This gives \(2x^2+3x-9=0\), hence \(x=\frac32\) or \(x=-3\). The valid interior value is \(x=\frac32\). Then for \(R(x,-y)\), \(y=-\sqrt{9-(\frac32)^2}=-\sqrt{\frac{27}{4}}=-\frac{3\sqrt3}{2}\).

text: Consider the complex number u = -1 + sqrt(3)i. Show its exponential form, find the least positive integer n such that u^n is real, find roots of related polynomial equations, and solve z^2 = 2 conjugate(z).

stem_blocks.text: Consider the complex number \(u=-1+\sqrt3 i\).
Consider the equation \(z^3+5z^2+10z+12=0\), where \(z\in\mathbb C\).
Consider the equation \(z^2=2z^*\), where \(z\in\mathbb C\) and \(z!=0\).

blocks.text: By finding the modulus and argument of \(u\), show that \(u=2e^{(2\pi i)/3}\).
Find the smallest positive integer \(n\) such that \(u^n\) is a real number.
Find the value of \(u^n\) when \(n\) takes the value found in part (b)(i).
Given that \(u\) is a root of \(z^3+5z^2+10z+12=0\), find the other roots.
By using a suitable transformation from \(z\) to \(w\), or otherwise, find the roots of \(1+5w+10w^2+12w^3=0\), where \(w\in\mathbb C\).
By expressing \(z\) in the form \(a+bi\), find the roots of \(z^2=2z^*\).

parts.label: b.i

parts.text: Find the value of \(u^n\) when \(n\) takes the value found in part (b)(i).

parts.label: c.i
parts.text: Given that \(u\) is a root of \(z^3+5z^2+10z+12=0\), find the other roots.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.text: By using a suitable transformation from \(z\) to \(w\), or otherwise, find the roots of \(1+5w+10w^2+12w^3=0\), where \(w\in\mathbb C\).

parts.text: By expressing \(z\) in the form \(a+bi\), find the roots of \(z^2=2z^*\).

answers.text: The other roots are \(-1-\sqrt3 i\) and \(-3\).
The roots are \(-\frac13\), \(\frac{-1+\sqrt3 i}{4}\), and \(\frac{-1-\sqrt3 i}{4}\).
The roots are \(2\), \(-1+\sqrt3 i\), and \(-1-\sqrt3 i\).

solution.outline: Use modulus-argument form and De Moivre's theorem, then use conjugate roots, reciprocal transformation and Cartesian-form complex algebra.

rows.text: Calculate \(|u|=\sqrt{(-1)^2+(\sqrt3)^2}=2\). The reference angle is \(\pi/3\), and since \(u\) is in the second quadrant, \(\arg u=\pi-\pi/3=2\pi/3\). Hence \(u=2e^{(2\pi i)/3}\). A convincing labelled diagram may also justify the argument.

mark_points.description: Finds the modulus \(|u|=2\).
Uses a valid reference-angle or diagram method for the argument.
Obtains \(\arg u=2\pi/3\) and hence \(u=2e^{(2\pi i)/3}\).

rows.text: Using \(u^n=2^n e^{(2n\pi i)/3}\), \(u^n\) is real when \(2n\pi/3=k\pi\), \(k\in\mathbb Z\), equivalently when \(n\) is a multiple of 3. The smallest positive integer is \(n=3\).

mark_points.description: Notes that the imaginary part must vanish, for example \(\sin(2n\pi/3)=0\) or \(2n\pi/3=k\pi\).
Recognizes or tests a multiple of 3 for \(n\).
Obtains the smallest positive integer \(n=3\).

rows.text: Substitute \(n=3\): \(u^3=2^3\cos(2\pi)=8\).

mark_points.description: Substitutes the valid multiple-of-3 value into \(u^n\).
Obtains \(u^3=8\).

rows.text: Since the polynomial has real coefficients and \(u=-1+\sqrt3 i\) is a root, \(-1-\sqrt3 i\) is also a root. Let the remaining real root be \(c\). Using the sum of roots gives \((-1+\sqrt3 i)+(-1-\sqrt3 i)+c=-5\), so \(-2+c=-5\) and \(c=-3\). Equivalently, the product of roots or coefficient comparison may be used.

mark_points.description: Identifies \(-1-\sqrt3 i\) as a root by the conjugate-root theorem, or equivalent exponential form.
Uses a valid method such as sum of roots, product of roots, or coefficient comparison to find the remaining real root.
Forms a correct relation using the conjugate pair, such as \((-1+\sqrt3 i)+(-1-\sqrt3 i)+c=-5\) or \((-1+\sqrt3 i)(-1-\sqrt3 i)c=-12\).
Simplifies the relation correctly, for example \(-2+c=-5\) or \(4c=-12\).
Obtains the remaining root \(z=-3\).

rows.text: Comparing \(z^3+5z^2+10z+12=0\) with \(1+5w+10w^2+12w^3=0\) gives the reciprocal transformation \(z=1/w\), so \(w=1/z\). Hence \(w=-1/3\) and \(w=1/(-1\pm\sqrt3 i)=(-1\mp\sqrt3 i)/4\), equivalently the complex roots are \((-1\pm\sqrt3 i)/4\). Factorization \(1+5w+10w^2+12w^3=(3w+1)(4w^2+2w+1)\) is an accepted route.

mark_points.description: Uses the reciprocal transformation \(z=1/w\), equivalently \(w=1/z\), or an equivalent two-mark transformation comparison.
Obtains the real root \(w=-1/3\), or the equivalent factor \(3w+1\).
Obtains one complex root \((-1+\sqrt3 i)/4\) or equivalent reciprocal form.
Obtains the conjugate complex root \((-1-\sqrt3 i)/4\) or equivalent reciprocal form.

rows.text: Let \(z=a+bi\), so \(z^*=a-bi\). Then \((a+bi)^2=2(a-bi)\), giving \(a^2-b^2+2abi=2a-2bi\). Equating parts gives \(a^2-b^2=2a\) and \(2ab=-2b\), so \(2b(a+1)=0\). If \(b=0\), then \(a^2=2a\) and, since \(z!=0\), \(a=2\). If \(a=-1\), then \(1-b^2=-2\), so \(b=\pm\sqrt3\). The roots are \(2\) and \(-1\pm\sqrt3 i\).

Expands and equates real and imaginary parts.
Attempts to solve for \(a\) or \(b\), for example from \(2b(a+1)=0\).
Obtains the real root \(z=2\), excluding \(z=0\).
Obtains the complex roots \(-1+\sqrt3 i\) and \(-1-\sqrt3 i\).

solution.outline: Differentiate f(x)=e^(cos 2x) with the chain rule to get f'(x)=(-2sin 2x)e^(cos 2x). Setting f'(x)=0 gives x=0, pi/2, pi in the interval, producing the coordinates (0,e), (pi/2,1/e), and (pi,e). Differentiate again using the product rule to classify x=0 and x=pi as maxima and x=pi/2 as a minimum. Sketch the curve on 0<=x<=pi with these extrema and the relative gradient-change behavior. Use the cosine Maclaurin series to obtain cos 2x=1-2x^2+(2/3)x^4+..., substitute cos 2x-1 into the exponential series to get e^(cos 2x-1)=1-2x^2+(8/3)x^4+..., then multiply by e to get f(x)=e-2ex^2+(8e/3)x^4+... . Finally use f(x)≈e(1-2x^2) on 0 to 1/10 and integrate to obtain 149e/1500.

answers.text: (cos theta+i sin theta)^5 = cos^5(theta)+5i cos^4(theta)sin(theta)+10i^2 cos^3(theta)sin^2(theta)+10i^3 cos^2(theta)sin^3(theta)+5i^4 cos(theta)sin^4(theta)+i^5 sin^5(theta). Hence the real part is cos^5(theta)-10cos^3(theta)sin^2(theta)+5cos(theta)sin^4(theta), and the imaginary part is 5cos^4(theta)sin(theta)-10cos^2(theta)sin^3(theta)+sin^5(theta).

By De Moivre's theorem, (cos theta+i sin theta)^5=cos(5theta)+i sin(5theta). Equating imaginary parts gives sin(5theta)=5cos^4(theta)sin(theta)-10cos^2(theta)sin^3(theta)+sin^5(theta). Substituting cos^2(theta)=1-sin^2(theta) and simplifying gives sin(5theta)=16sin^5(theta)-20sin^3(theta)+5sin(theta).
Factor sin(5theta)=sin(theta)(16sin^4(theta)-20sin^2(theta)+5). For theta=pi/5 and theta=3pi/5, sin(5theta)=0 while sin(theta) is not 0, so both angles satisfy 16sin^4(theta)-20sin^2(theta)+5=0.

Let u=sin^2(theta). Solving 16u^2-20u+5=0 gives u=(5+-sqrt(5))/8. Thus sin(pi/5)sin(3pi/5)=sqrt((5-sqrt(5))/8)*sqrt((5+sqrt(5))/8)=sqrt(20/64)=sqrt(5)/4. Equivalently, use the product of roots of the quartic together with sin(pi/5)=sin(4pi/5) and sin(2pi/5)=sin(3pi/5).

Attempts to integrate the partial-fraction expression. Obtains f(x)=(1/k)(ln|x|-ln|k-x|)+c, awarding one mark for each logarithmic term. Separates variables and integrates both sides. Obtains an equivalent logarithmic relation after integration. Substitutes t=0 and P=1200 to determine the integration constant, or uses the equivalent exponential form. Obtains the corresponding constant relation from the initial condition. Forms the exponential relation involving P/(k-P). Attempts to rearrange the relation and isolate P. Obtains an equivalent isolated expression for P. Shows P=1200k/((k-1200)e^(-t/5)+1200). Substitutes t=10 and P=2400 into the derived model. Forms the resulting equation in k. text: A function f is defined by f(x) = arcsin((x^2 - 1)/(x^2 + 1)), where x is real. A function g is defined by g(x) = arcsin((x^2 - 1)/(x^2 + 1)), where x is real and x >= 0.

blocks.text: Show that f is an even function.
By considering limits, show that the graph of y = f(x) has a horizontal asymptote and state its equation.
(i) Show that f'(x) = 2x/(sqrt(x^2)(x^2 + 1)) for x real, x != 0. (ii) By using the expression for f'(x) and the result sqrt(x^2) = |x|, show that f is decreasing for x < 0.
Find an expression for g^(-1)(x), justifying your answer.
State the domain of g^(-1).
Sketch the graph of y = g^(-1)(x), clearly indicating any asymptotes with their equations and stating the values of any axes intercepts.

answers.text: f is even, since f(-x) = f(x).
As x -> +/-infinity, f(x) -> arcsin(1) = pi/2, so the horizontal asymptote is y = pi/2.
(i) f'(x) = 2x/(sqrt(x^2)(x^2 + 1)) for x != 0. (ii) For x < 0, |x| = -x, so f'(x) = -2/(x^2 + 1) < 0; hence f is decreasing for x < 0.
g^(-1)(x) = sqrt((1 + sin x)/(1 - sin x)).
The graph has domain [-pi/2, pi/2), range y >= 0, y-intercept y = 1, x-intercept at x = -pi/2, and vertical asymptote x = pi/2.

rows.text: Either show f(-x) = arcsin(((-x)^2 - 1)/((-x)^2 + 1)) = arcsin((x^2 - 1)/(x^2 + 1)) = f(x), or use a sketch with y-axis symmetry, then conclude f is even.

rows.text: Use the quotient rule on (x^2 - 1)/(x^2 + 1) to obtain 4x/(x^2 + 1)^2. Use the chain rule for arcsin u, so f'(x) = [1/sqrt(1-u^2)] * [4x/(x^2 + 1)^2]. This simplifies to 4x/sqrt((x^2 + 1)^2 - (x^2 - 1)^2) * 1/(x^2 + 1) = 4x/sqrt(4x^2) * 1/(x^2 + 1) = 2x/(sqrt(x^2)(x^2 + 1)). For x < 0, |x| = -x, hence f'(x) = -2/(x^2 + 1), or equivalently the numerator is negative and the denominator is positive. Therefore f'(x) < 0, so f is decreasing for x < 0.

rows.text: Let x = arcsin((y^2 - 1)/(y^2 + 1)). Then sin x = (y^2 - 1)/(y^2 + 1), so y^2 sin x + sin x = y^2 - 1. Hence y^2 = (1 + sin x)/(1 - sin x). Since the domain of g is y real, y >= 0, the range of g^(-1) must be y real, y >= 0; therefore the positive root is taken. Thus g^(-1)(x) = sqrt((1 + sin x)/(1 - sin x)).

text: Consider a triangle \(ABC\), where \(AC=12\), \(CB=7\) and \(\angle BAC=25^\circ\). Find the smallest possible perimeter of triangle \(ABC\).

blocks.text: Find the smallest possible perimeter of triangle \(ABC\).

parts.label: main
parts.text: Find the smallest possible perimeter of triangle \(ABC\).

solution.outline: Use the cosine rule or sine rule to identify the possible triangle configurations, choose the smaller possible third side, and add the three sides.

rows.text:
EITHER

attempt to use cosine rule \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(12^2+AB^2-2\times12\times\cos25^\circ\times AB=7^2\) OR \(AB^2-21.7513\ldots AB+95=0\) \(\quad\mathrm{(A1)}\)

at least one correct value for \(AB\) \(\quad\mathrm{(A1)}\)

\(AB=6.05068\ldots\) OR \(AB=15.7007\ldots\)

using their smaller value for \(AB\) to find minimum perimeter \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(12+7+6.05068\ldots\)

OR

attempt to use sine rule \(\quad\mathrm{(M1)}\)

\(\dfrac{\sin B}{12}=\dfrac{\sin25^\circ}{7}\) OR \(\sin B=0.724488\ldots\) OR \(\widehat{B}=133.573\ldots^\circ\) OR \(\widehat{B}=46.4263\ldots^\circ\) \(\quad\mathrm{(A1)}\)

at least one correct value for \(\widehat{C}\)

text: A marsupial population P on a remote island is modelled by the logistic differential equation dP/dt = kP(1-P/N), where t is measured in years and k,N are positive constants. N is the maximum sustainable population. Students interpret dP/dt, prove the second-derivative form, justify the maximum growth rate, solve the logistic equation, and use P(10)=3P0 with N=4P0 to find k.

stem_blocks.text: The population, P, of a particular species of marsupial on a small remote island can be modelled by the logistic differential equation dP/dt = kP(1-P/N).
Here t is the time measured in years and k and N are positive constants. The constant N represents the maximum population that the island can sustain indefinitely.
Let P0 be the initial population of marsupials. After 10 years, the population is 3P0. It is known that N=4P0.

blocks.text: In the context of the population model, interpret the meaning of dP/dt.
Show that d2P/dt2 = k^2 P(1-P/N)(1-2P/N).
Hence show that the population of marsupials will increase at its maximum rate when P=N/2. Justify your answer.
Hence determine the maximum value of dP/dt in terms of k and N.
By solving the logistic differential equation, show that its solution can be expressed in the form kt = ln((P/P0)((N-P0)/(N-P))).
Find the value of k for this population model.

answers.text: dP/dt is the rate of change of the marsupial population with respect to time.
Differentiate dP/dt=kP(1-P/N), substitute dP/dt back into the result, and simplify to k^2P(1-P/N)(1-2P/N).
Set the second derivative to zero to get P=0, N/2, N; use a sign diagram, sketch, or second-derivative evidence to justify that dP/dt has a local maximum at P=N/2.
Substitute P=N/2 into dP/dt=kP(1-P/N) to obtain the maximum value kN/4.
Separate variables and integrate using partial fractions, or an equivalent substitution, then use P=P0 when t=0 to obtain kt=ln((P/P0)((N-P0)/(N-P))).
Substitute t=10, P=3P0 and N=4P0 into the result: 10k=ln 9, so k=(ln 9)/10=0.220 to three significant figures.

solution.outline: Use the logistic equation and its derivative to locate the maximum growth rate at P=N/2, then solve the separable logistic differential equation and substitute P(10)=3P0 with N=4P0.

A large group of employees work more than 40 hours per week. (i) An employee is selected at random from this large group. Find the probability that this employee works less than 55 hours per week. (ii) Ten employees are selected at random from this large group. Find the probability that exactly five of them work less than 55 hours per week.
Find the maximum time, in hours per week, that an employee can work and still be considered part-time.

solution.outline: Use the normal model for T to find P(T>40), then multiply independent probabilities for the ordered group event. For employees already known to work more than 40 hours, use conditional probability and then a binomial model for ten employees. For the part-time threshold, express the two tails around the central 0.904 region in the ratio 1:2, find P(T<a)=0.032, and invert the normal distribution to get a.

text: A three-dimensional vectors question about points A(1,2,3), B(k,-2,1) and C(5,0,2). Students find vectors, prove collinearity when k=9, write a vector equation for the line through A, B and C, prove another line is skew to it, find the plane through A, B and C when k is not 9, and find the point on that plane closest to the origin.

stem_blocks.text: Consider the points A(1,2,3), B(k,-2,1) and C(5,0,2), where k is real.
For k=9, let L1 be the line passing through A, B and C. Line L2 has equation (x-1)/2 = y/3 = 1-z.
For k not equal to 9, let Pi be the plane containing A, B and C.

blocks.text: Write down vector AB and vector AC.
Given that the points A, B and C lie on a straight line, show that k=9.
For k=9, find a vector equation of the line L1 passing through A, B and C.
Line L2 has the equation (x-1)/2 = y/3 = 1-z. Show that the lines L1 and L2 are skew.
For k not equal to 9, find the Cartesian equation of the plane Pi containing A, B and C.
Find the coordinates of the point on the plane Pi which is closest to the origin (0,0,0).

parts.label: b

parts.label: c.i

parts.label: c.ii

parts.label: d.ii
parts.text: Find the coordinates of the point on the plane Pi which is closest to the origin (0,0,0).

answers.text: If A, B and C are collinear, AB is a scalar multiple of AC. Comparing the second and third components gives AB=2AC, so k-1=2*4 and hence k=9.
For k=9, a direction vector for L1 is AC=(4,-2,-1). Hence L1 can be written as r=(1,2,3)+lambda(4,-2,-1), or an equivalent vector equation.

A point on L1 is (1+4lambda,2-2lambda,3-lambda). From L2, write r=(1,0,1)+mu(2,3,-1), so a point on L2 is (1+2mu,3mu,1-mu). Equating coordinates gives 1+4lambda=1+2mu, 2-2lambda=3mu and 3-lambda=1-mu. Solving two equations gives values such as lambda=1/4 and mu=1/2, which do not satisfy the third equation. The direction vectors (4,-2,-1) and (2,3,-1) are not scalar multiples, so the lines do not meet and are not parallel; hence they are skew.
Using AB=(k-1,-4,-2) and AC=(4,-2,-1), AB cross AC=(0,k-9,18-2k)=(k-9)(0,1,-2). Substituting a point into the plane equation gives (k-9)y+2(9-k)z=36-4k, so since k is not 9 the plane is y-2z=-4.
The closest point lies on the normal line through the origin in direction (0,1,-2), so r=t(0,1,-2). Substitution into y-2z=-4 gives t+4t=-4, so t=-4/5. Therefore the point is (0,-0.8,1.6).

solution.outline: Find AB and AC, use collinearity to determine k=9, write L1 in vector form, compare L1 with L2 to show no intersection and no parallelism, find a normal vector to the plane by a cross product, derive the Cartesian plane equation, then intersect the plane with the normal line through the origin to find the closest point.

Assume \(p^2-8q-11=0\), \((p,q\in\mathbb Z)\quad\mathrm{M1}\)

Note: This \(\mathrm{M1}\) is dependent on the assumption of truth (implied by "assume" or "suppose that ... is true"). Subsequent marks should be awarded independently.

a contradiction as LHS is even and RHS is odd \(\quad\mathrm{R1}\)

Note: This \(\mathrm{R1}\) is dependent on all previous marks. Accept correct variations such as work based on \(p=2k-1\).

therefore, if \(p,q\in\mathbb Z\) then \(p^2-8q-11\) is not \(0\quad\mathrm{AG}\)

stem_blocks.text: An engineer is designing a gutter to catch rainwater from the roof of a house.
The gutter will be open at the top and is made by folding a piece of sheet metal 45 cm wide and 600 cm long.

The cross-section of the gutter is shaded in the diagram. The height of both vertical sides is 10 cm. The width of the gutter is w cm. Arc AB lies on the circumference of a circle with centre O and radius 12 cm.
Let angle AOB = theta radians, where 0 < theta < pi.

In a storm, the total volume, in cm^3, of rainwater that enters the gutter can be modelled by R(t), where t is the time in seconds since the start of the storm. The rate is R'(t)=50 cos(2pi t/5)+3000 for t>=0.
During any 60-second period, if the volume of rainwater entering the gutter is greater than the volume of the gutter, it will overflow.

blocks.text: Show that theta=2.08, correct to three significant figures.
Find the area of the cross-section of the gutter.
Determine whether the gutter overflowed in this storm. Justify your answer.

parts.label: b
parts.text: Find the area of the cross-section of the gutter.

parts.label: c
parts.text: Determine whether the gutter overflowed in this storm. Justify your answer.

answers.text: The curved arc length is 45-10-10=25 cm, so 25=12theta and theta=25/12=2.08 to three significant figures.
Using theta=2.08, w=2(12)sin(theta/2)=20.7 cm. The cross-sectional area is the rectangle 10w plus the circular segment area, giving approximately 294 cm^2.

The gutter volume is about 600 times the cross-sectional area, approximately 176000 cm^3. In any 60-second period the rainfall volume is integral of R'(t), equal to 180000 cm^3 because the cosine term completes whole periods. Since 180000 is greater than the gutter volume, the gutter overflowed.

classification_review.solving_path: Uses Euler recurrence y1=y0+h f(x0,y0). Obtains y1=2+0.1[1^2+3(2)^2]/2=2.65. Uses homogeneous substitution y=vx. Differentiates to dy/dx=v+x dv/dx. Substitutes and obtains a relation equivalent to x dv/dx=(1+2v^2)/v. Obtains x dv/dx=(1+2v^2)/v. Separates variables and integrates v/(2v^2+1) dv=1/x dx. Obtains (1/4)ln(2v^2+1)=ln(x)+C. Uses y(1)=2 to determine the integration constant. Obtains 2y^2/x^2+1=9x^4. Substitutes x=1.1 to obtain y=2.71422..., giving 2.71. States the solution curve is concave up, equivalently d^2y/dx^2>0, on 1 to 1.1. Explains that the Euler tangent lies below a concave-up curve, so Euler underestimates. Sketches an appropriate correct derivative graph, dy/dx or d^2y/dx^2. Obtains inflexion x=0.655996..., giving 0.656. Sets d^2y/dx^2=0 and obtains -x^4+x^2y^2+6y^4=0. Divides by an appropriate positive power product and substitutes m=y/x. Forms 6m^4+m^2-1=0. Factorizes as (3m^2-1)(2m^2+1)=0. Obtains m=plus or minus 1/sqrt(3). Uses x>0 and y>0 to select y=x/sqrt(3), so m=1/sqrt(3).

stem_blocks.text: Consider the differential equation dy/dx=(x^2+3y^2)/(xy), where x>0 and y>0. It is given that y=2 when x=1.
The graph of y=x sqrt((9x^4-1)/2) for sqrt(3)/3<x<1 has a point of inflexion at the point P. It can be shown that d2y/dx2=(-x^4+x^2y^2+6y^4)/(x^2y^3), where x>0 and y>0.

answers.text: Let y=vx. Then dy/dx=v+x dv/dx and x dv/dx=(1+2v^2)/v. Separating and integrating gives (1/4)ln(2v^2+1)=ln x+C. Using x=1,y=2 gives the constant and hence y=x sqrt((9x^4-1)/2).
Substituting x=1.1 gives y=2.71422..., so y=2.71.
The graph is concave up, equivalently d2y/dx2>0 on 1<=x<=1.1. Therefore the tangent used in Euler's method gives an underestimate, so the exact value at x=1.1 is greater than the Euler approximation.
A correct sketch of dy/dx or d2y/dx2 identifies the inflexion at x=0.655996..., so x=0.656.
At P, d2y/dx2=0, so -x^4+x^2y^2+6y^4=0. Dividing by powers of x and y, or factorizing, gives (3m^2-1)(2m^2+1)=0 with m=y/x. Since x>0 and y>0, m=1/sqrt(3), so P lies on y=(1/sqrt(3))x.

answers.text: Using Euler's method with step size 0.1 gives y1 = 2.02 and y5 = 2.098 to four significant figures.
Solving dy/dx = (4 - y)/10 with y(0) = 2 gives y = 4 - 2e^(-x/10).
The absolute error is 0.000479, equivalently 4.79 x 10^-4. Using the four-significant-figure value gives 0.000459.

solution.outline: Use Euler's recursive formula to approximate y at x = 0.5, solve the first-order differential equation exactly using separation of variables or an integrating factor, then compare the Euler value with the exact value.

rows.text: Attempt to use the recursive formula y_n = y_(n-1) + 0.1((4 - y_(n-1))/10). Euler table values include y1 = 2.02, y2 = 2.0398, y3 = 2.05940..., y4 = 2.07880..., y5 = 2.09801..., so y5 = 2.098 to four significant figures. Accept any answer which rounds to the correct four-significant-figure value; no marks for a final answer of 2.1 or 2.10 with no working.

rows.text: Method 1: separate variables and integrate: integral dy/(4 - y) = integral dx/10, giving -ln|4 - y| = x/10 + c. Substitute x = 0, y = 2 to find c = -ln 2, then obtain |4 - y| = 2e^(-x/10) or 4 - y = Ae^(-x/10), and hence y = 4 - 2e^(-x/10). Method 2: rearrange to dy/dx + (1/10)y = 4/10, use integrating factor e^(x/10), obtain e^(x/10)y = 4e^(x/10) + c, substitute x = 0, y = 2 to find c = -2, and hence y = 4 - 2e^(-x/10).

text: A farmer is growing a field of wheat plants. The height H cm of each plant is normally distributed. Given lower and upper tail probabilities, find the middle probability, the normal parameters, binomial probabilities for 100 plants, a conditional probability, and a standard deviation from an interquartile range.

stem_blocks.text: A farmer is growing a field of wheat plants. The height, H cm, of each plant can be modelled by a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\).
The farmer measures 100 randomly selected plants. Any plant with a height greater than 98.1 cm is considered ready to harvest. Heights of plants are independent of each other.

In another field, the farmer is growing the same variety of wheat, but is using a different fertilizer. The heights of these plants, F cm, are normally distributed with mean 98.6 and standard deviation d. The farmer finds the interquartile range to be 4.82 cm.

blocks.text: Find the probability that the height of a randomly selected plant is between 94.6 cm and 98.1 cm.
Find the value of \(\mu\) and the value of \(\sigma\).
Find the probability that exactly 34 plants are ready to harvest.
Given that fewer than 49 plants are ready to harvest, find the probability that exactly 34 plants are ready to harvest.
Find the value of \(d\).

answers.text: Solving the component equations gives s=2 and t=-1; substituting gives A with position vector (5, 8, 9).

rows.text: Method 1: sketch y = x^2/(x - 3) = x + 3 + 9/(x - 3). The oblique asymptote has gradient 1, so the maximum value of m is 1. Considering a straight line steeper than the horizontal line through (-3, 0) and (0, 0) gives m > 0, hence 0 < m <= 1. Method 2: eliminate y to get x^2 = m(x^2 - 9), so (m - 1)x^2 - 9m = 0. Solving for no real intersection gives 0 < m < 1, then a valid reason shows m = 1 also gives no solution, so 0 < m <= 1.

Using the graph or derivative information, the amount of salt is decreasing most rapidly at t=12.9 minutes.
Integrate x(t)/(t+1) from 0 to 60, or compute total salt entering minus x(60). The amount of salt that left the tank is 36.7 g.

text: Use the double-angle identity for tangent to verify roots and derive exact trigonometric values.

stem_blocks.text: This question concerns the tangent double-angle identity, related quadratic roots and exact trigonometric values.

blocks.text: Show that \(\cot 2\theta=\dfrac{1-\tan^2\theta}{2\tan\theta}\).
Verify that \(x=\tan\theta\) and \(x=-\cot\theta\) satisfy the equation \(x^2+(2\cot 2\theta)x-1=0\).
Hence, or otherwise, show that the exact value of \(\tan\frac{\pi}{12}=2-\sqrt3\).
Using the results from parts (b) and (c), find the exact value of \(\tan\frac{\pi}{24}-\cot\frac{\pi}{24}\). Give your answer in the form \(a+b\sqrt3\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\).

parts.label: a
parts.text: Show that \(\cot 2\theta=\dfrac{1-\tan^2\theta}{2\tan\theta}\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Verify that \(x=\tan\theta\) and \(x=-\cot\theta\) satisfy the equation \(x^2+(2\cot 2\theta)x-1=0\).

parts.label: c
parts.text: Hence, or otherwise, show that the exact value of \(\tan\frac{\pi}{12}=2-\sqrt3\).

parts.label: d
parts.text: Using the results from parts (b) and (c), find the exact value of \(\tan\frac{\pi}{24}-\cot\frac{\pi}{24}\). Give your answer in the form \(a+b\sqrt3\) where \(a,b\in\mathbb Z\).

answers.text: Substitution of \(x=\tan\theta\) gives zero using part (a). Substitution of \(x=-\cot\theta\) also gives zero, or equivalently the two proposed values have sum \(-2\cot2\theta\) and product \(-1\), matching the quadratic.
With \(\theta=\pi/12\), the root equation is \(x^2+2\sqrt3x-1=0\), so \(x=-\sqrt3\pm2\). Since \(\tan(\pi/12)>0\), \(\tan(\pi/12)=2-\sqrt3\).
The expression is the sum of the roots of \(x^2+(2\cot(\pi/12))x-1=0\), so \(\tan(\pi/24)-\cot(\pi/24)=-2\cot(\pi/12)=-\dfrac{2}{2-\sqrt3}=-4-2\sqrt3\).

solution.outline: Use the reciprocal relationship between cotangent and tangent plus the tangent double-angle identity, verify the proposed roots, substitute theta=pi/12 to obtain tan(pi/12), then use the sum of roots at theta=pi/24 and rationalise.

text: This question asks you to explore the behaviour and key features of cubic polynomials of the form \(x^3-3cx+d\). Consider \(f(x)=x^3-3cx+2\) for \(x\in\mathbb R\), where \(c\in\mathbb R\). The graphs of \(y=f(x)\) for \(c=-1\) and \(c=0\) are shown below.

parts.label: a.i
parts.text: On separate axes, sketch the graph of \(y=f(x)\) showing the value of the \(y\)-intercept and the coordinates of any points with zero gradient, for \(c=1\).

parts.label: a.ii
parts.text: On separate axes, sketch the graph of \(y=f(x)\) showing the value of the \(y\)-intercept and the coordinates of any points with zero gradient, for \(c=2\).

parts.label: b
parts.text: Write down an expression for \(f'(x)\).

parts.label: c.i
parts.text: Hence, or otherwise, find the set of values of \(c\) such that the graph of \(y=f(x)\) has a point of inflexion with zero gradient.

parts.label: c.ii
parts.text: Hence, or otherwise, find the set of values of \(c\) such that the graph of \(y=f(x)\) has one local maximum point and one local minimum point.

parts.label: c.iii
parts.text: Hence, or otherwise, find the set of values of \(c\) such that the graph of \(y=f(x)\) has no points where the gradient is equal to zero.

parts.label: d.i
parts.text: Given that the graph of \(y=f(x)\) has one local maximum point and one local minimum point, show that the \(y\)-coordinate of the local maximum point is \(2c^{3/2}+2\).

parts.label: d.ii
parts.text: Given that the graph of \(y=f(x)\) has one local maximum point and one local minimum point, show that the \(y\)-coordinate of the local minimum point is \(-2c^{3/2}+2\).

parts.label: e.i
parts.text: Hence, for \(c>0\), find the set of values of \(c\) such that the graph of \(y=f(x)\) has exactly one \(x\)-axis intercept.

parts.label: e.ii
parts.text: Hence, for \(c>0\), find the set of values of \(c\) such that the graph of \(y=f(x)\) has exactly two \(x\)-axis intercepts.

parts.label: e.iii
parts.text: Hence, for \(c>0\), find the set of values of \(c\) such that the graph of \(y=f(x)\) has exactly three \(x\)-axis intercepts.

parts.label: f
parts.text: Consider the function \(g(x)=x^3-3cx+d\) for \(x\in\mathbb{R}\), where \(c,d\in\mathbb{R}\). Find all conditions on \(c\) and \(d\) such that the graph of \(y=g(x)\) has exactly one \(x\)-axis intercept, explaining your reasoning.

Factorizes or divides to solve for x. Obtains x=2/cos(pi/n). Substitutes x into perimeter or area. Obtains A=P=4n tan(pi/n). Uses Maclaurin series for tan x with x=pi/n. Expands 4n tan(pi/n) with vanishing inverse-power terms. Limit is 4pi. Interprets the limit as a circle of radius 2 (area and perimeter 4pi). Uses A=(1/2)ab and P=a+b+sqrt(a^2+b^2). Equates A=P. text: This Paper 3 question investigates polygons for which the numerical area equals the numerical perimeter. Students solve the square case, derive regular n-gon formulae using an isosceles-triangle decomposition, interpret the limiting value as a circle of radius 2, then characterize two integer right triangles with area equal to perimeter.

stem_blocks.text: This question asks you to examine polygons for which the numerical value of the area is the same as the numerical value of the perimeter. Let the numerical value of area be A and perimeter be P.

An n-sided regular polygon is divided into n congruent isosceles triangles. Let x be the equal side length, y the third side length, and the included angle be 2*pi/n. Later, consider a right-angled triangle with side lengths a, b and sqrt(a^2+b^2), where a>=b, such that A=P.

blocks.text: Find the side length s, where s>0, of a square such that A=P.
Write down, in terms of x and n, an expression for the area A_T of one of these isosceles triangles.
Show that y=2x sin(pi/n).
Use the results from parts (b) and (c) to show that A=P=4n tan(pi/n).
Use the Maclaurin series for tan x to find lim as n tends to infinity of 4n tan(pi/n).
Interpret your answer to part (e)(i) geometrically.
Consider a right-angled triangle with side lengths a, b and sqrt(a^2+b^2), where a>=b, such that A=P. Show that a=8/(b-4)+4.
By using the result of part (f) or otherwise, determine the three side lengths of the only two right-angled triangles for which a, b, A and P are integers.
Determine the area and perimeter of these two right-angled triangles.

answers.text: A_T=(1/2)x^2 sin(2*pi/n), or an equivalent expression in x and n.
Geometrically, the regular polygon tends to a circle of radius 2, with area and perimeter both tending to 4*pi.
Using A=(1/2)ab and P=a+b+sqrt(a^2+b^2), A=P leads to a=8/(b-4)+4.
The two right-angled triangles have side lengths (5,12,13) and (6,8,10).

solution.outline: Solve the square case directly. For the regular polygon, use the area of one isosceles triangle and the side relation y=2x sin(pi/n); imposing A=P gives x=2/cos(pi/n) and hence A=P=4n tan(pi/n). The Maclaurin series gives the limit 4pi, interpreted as a circle of radius 2. For right triangles, equate area and perimeter, isolate and square the hypotenuse expression, derive a=8/(b-4)+4, then find the two integer triples and their common area/perimeter values.

answers.text: An inverted parabola y=x(2-x) passing through x-intercepts 0 and 2, with local maximum at (1,1).
For n=3 and n=5: 1 local maximum, 0 local minima, 2 points of inflexion with zero gradient. For n=2 and n=4: 1 local maximum, 2 local minima, 0 points of inflexion with zero gradient.
Using the product rule, f'_n(x)=-n x^n(a-x)^(n-1)+n x^(n-1)(a-x)^n, which factorizes to n x^(n-1)(a-2x)(a-x)^(n-1).
f_n(a/2)=(a/2)^n(a/2)^n=(a/2)^(2n)>0, since a>0 and n is a positive integer; hence (a/2, f_n(a/2)) is above the horizontal axis.
f'_n(a/4)=n(a/4)^(n-1)(a/2)(3a/4)^(n-1), and every factor is positive, so f'_n(a/4)>0.
For even n, f'_n(-1)=n(-1)^(n-1)(a+2)(a+1)^(n-1)<0, while f'_n(0)=0 and f'_n(a/4)>0. Therefore the gradient changes from negative to positive at (0,0), so it is a local minimum.

For odd n, f'_n(-1)=n(-1)^(n-1)(a+2)(a+1)^(n-1)>0, while f'_n(0)=0 and f'_n(a/4)>0. Therefore there is a zero gradient at (0,0) without a maximum or minimum, so it is a point of inflexion with zero gradient.

classification_review.solving_path: Expands (omega-1)(omega^2+omega+1) or uses polynomial division. Obtains omega^3-1. Uses omega^3=1 and omega is not 1. Deduces omega^2+omega+1=0. Finds either P0P1 or P0P2 by a valid geometric, trigonometric, coordinate, or complex method. Obtains P0P1=sqrt(3). Obtains P0P2=sqrt(3), hence their product is 3. Uses z^4-1=(z-1)(z^3+z^2+z+1), or an equivalent root-sum method. Uses omega^4=1 and omega is not 1 to deduce omega^3+omega^2+omega+1=0. Obtains P0P2=2. Finds either P0P1 or P0P3 by a valid method. Obtains P0P1=sqrt(2). Obtains P0P3=sqrt(2), hence P0P1 times P0P2 times P0P3 equals 4. Suggests P0P1 times P0P2 times ... times P0P(n-1) equals n. Writes P0P2=|1-omega^2|. Writes P0P3=|1-omega^3|. Writes P0P(n-1)=|1-omega^(n-1)|. Considers z^(n-1)+z^(n-2)+...+z+1=0. Identifies its roots as omega, omega^2, ..., omega^(n-1). Obtains z^(n-1)+...+z+1=(z-omega)(z-omega^2)...(z-omega^(n-1)). text: In this question you will be exploring the strategies required to solve a system of linear differential equations. Consider dx/dt=x-y and dy/dt=ax+y, where x, y and t are positive real numbers and a is a parameter. First consider a=0, then a=-1, then a=-4.

stem_blocks.text: In this question you will be exploring the strategies required to solve a system of linear differential equations.
Consider the system dx/dt=x-y and dy/dt=ax+y, where x, y and t are positive real numbers and a is a parameter.
First consider a=0, then a=-1, then a=-4.

blocks.text: For a=0, by solving dy/dt=y, show that y=Ae^t where A is a constant.
Show that dx/dt-x=-Ae^t.
Solve the differential equation in part (a)(ii) to find x as a function of t.
For a=-1, by differentiating dy/dt=-x+y with respect to t, show that d^2y/dt^2=2dy/dt.
By substituting Y=dy/dt, show that Y=Be^(2t) where B is a constant.
Hence find y as a function of t.
Hence show that x=-(B/2)e^(2t)+C, where C is a constant.
For a=-4, show that d^2y/dt^2-2dy/dt-3y=0.

From previous cases, we might conjecture that a solution to this differential equation is y=Fe^(lambda t), where lambda is real and F is a constant. Find the two values for lambda that satisfy d^2y/dt^2-2dy/dt-3y=0.
Let the two values found in part (c)(ii) be lambda_1 and lambda_2. Verify that y=Fe^(lambda_1 t)+Ge^(lambda_2 t) is a solution to the differential equation in part (c)(i), where G is a constant.

answers.text: Separating variables gives integral dy/y=integral dt, so ln y=t+c and hence y=Ae^t.
Substitute y=Ae^t into dx/dt=x-y to obtain dx/dt=x-Ae^t, hence dx/dt-x=-Ae^t.
Using integrating factor e^(-t), d(xe^(-t))/dt=-A. Hence xe^(-t)=-At+D and x=(-At+D)e^t.
Differentiating dy/dt=-x+y gives d^2y/dt^2=-dx/dt+dy/dt. With a=-1, dx/dt=x-y and dy/dt=-x+y, so d^2y/dt^2=2dy/dt.
Let Y=dy/dt. Then dY/dt=2Y, so integral dY/Y=integral 2dt, giving ln Y=2t+c and Y=Be^(2t).
Substitute dy/dt=Be^(2t) and y=(B/2)e^(2t)+C into dy/dt=-x+y to obtain x=-(B/2)e^(2t)+C.
For a=-4, dy/dt=-4x+y and d^2y/dt^2=-4dx/dt+dy/dt. Eliminating x using the system gives d^2y/dt^2=2dy/dt+3y, hence d^2y/dt^2-2dy/dt-3y=0.
For y=Fe^(lambda t), dy/dt=F lambda e^(lambda t) and d^2y/dt^2=F lambda^2 e^(lambda t). Substitution gives lambda^2-2lambda-3=0, so lambda=3 or lambda=-1.
With lambda values 3 and -1, y=Fe^(3t)+Ge^(-t). Then dy/dt=3Fe^(3t)-Ge^(-t) and d^2y/dt^2=9Fe^(3t)+Ge^(-t). Substitution into d^2y/dt^2-2dy/dt-3y simplifies to 0.

text: This Paper 3 question investigates polygonal numbers. Students verify the triangular-number formula, identify the 26th triangular number as 351, prove that two consecutive triangular numbers sum to a square number and represent the case n=4 with a diagram, show that 8P_3(n)+1 is an odd square, derive the pentagonal-number formula from an arithmetic series, find the smallest positive integer greater than 1 that is both triangular and pentagonal, and use induction to prove the general polygonal-number formula.

stem_blocks.text: This question asks you to explore some properties of polygonal numbers and to determine and prove interesting results involving these numbers. A polygonal number is an integer which can be represented as a series of dots arranged in the shape of a regular polygon. Triangular numbers, square numbers and pentagonal numbers are examples of polygonal numbers.

For example, a triangular number is a number that can be arranged in the shape of an equilateral triangle. The first five triangular numbers are 1, 3, 6, 10 and 15. The table illustrates the first five triangular, square and pentagonal numbers respectively; in each case the first polygonal number is represented by a single dot.

For an r-sided regular polygon, where r is a positive integer and r>=3, the nth polygonal number P_r(n) is given by P_r(n)=((r-2)n^2-(r-4)n)/2, where n is a positive integer. Hence, for square numbers, P_4(n)=n^2.

The nth pentagonal number can be represented by the arithmetic series P_5(n)=1+4+7+...+(3n-2). A polygonal number P_r(n) can be represented by the series sum from m=1 to n of (1+(m-1)(r-2)), where r is a positive integer and r>=3.

blocks.text: For triangular numbers, verify that P_3(n)=n(n+1)/2.
The number 351 is a triangular number. Determine which one it is.
Show that P_3(n)+P_3(n+1)=(n+1)^2.
State, in words, what the identity given in part (b)(i) shows for two consecutive triangular numbers.
For n=4, sketch a diagram clearly showing your answer to part (b)(ii).
Show that 8P_3(n)+1 is the square of an odd number for all positive integers n.
Hence show that P_5(n)=n(3n-1)/2 for positive integers n.
By using a suitable table of values or otherwise, determine the smallest positive integer, greater than 1, that is both a triangular number and a pentagonal number.
Use mathematical induction to prove that P_r(n)=((r-2)n^2-(r-4)n)/2, where n is a positive integer.

Prove the general formula by checking n=1, assuming n=k, adding the next series term, simplifying to the k+1 case, and concluding by induction.

text: This question asks you to explore cubic polynomials of the form (x-r)(x^2-2ax+a^2+b^2) for real x and corresponding cubic equations with one real root and two complex roots of the form (z-r)(z^2-2az+a^2+b^2)=0 for complex z.

stem_blocks.text: This question asks you to explore cubic polynomials of the form (x-r)(x^2-2ax+a^2+b^2) for real x and corresponding cubic equations with one real root and two complex roots of the form (z-r)(z^2-2az+a^2+b^2)=0 for complex z.
In parts (a), (b) and (c), let r=1, a=4 and b=1. Consider the equation (z-1)(z^2-8z+17)=0 for complex z.
Consider g(x)=(x-r)(x^2-2ax+a^2+b^2) for real x, where r and a are real and b is real with b>0.
On the Cartesian plane, C1(a,sqrt(g'(a))) and C2(a,-sqrt(g'(a))) represent the real and imaginary parts of the complex roots.

Sketch the curve y=f(x) and the tangent to the curve at point A, clearly showing where the tangent crosses the x-axis.

Hence, or otherwise, prove that the tangent to the curve y=g(x) at the point A(a,g(a)) intersects the x-axis at the point R(r,0).
The equation (z-r)(z^2-2az+a^2+b^2)=0 has roots r and a+-bi. Deduce from part (d)(i) that the complex roots can be expressed as a+-i sqrt(g'(a)).
Use the diagram for y=(x-r)(x^2-2ax+a^2+16), tangent point A(a,80), and x-axis intersection R(-2,0), to determine the roots of the corresponding equation (z-r)(z^2-2az+a^2+16)=0.

answers.text: f'(x)=(x-1)(2x-8)+x^2-8x+17=3x^2-18x+25, so f'(4)=1. Since A(4,3) lies on y=x-1, the line y=x-1 is the tangent at A.
A positive cubic with x-intercept x=1 and local maximum and local minimum in the first quadrant to the left of A; the tangent passes through A and crosses the x-axis at x=1.
g(a)=b^2(a-r) and g'(a)=b^2. The tangent at A is y-b^2(a-r)=b^2(x-a), hence y=b^2(x-r). Setting y=0 gives x=r since b>0, so the tangent intersects the x-axis at R(r,0).
Since g'(a)=b^2 and b>0, b=sqrt(g'(a)), so the complex roots are a+-i sqrt(g'(a)).
Here b=4 and r=-2. Using A(a,80) on the tangent y=16(x-r) gives 80=16(a+2), so a=3. The roots are -2 and 3+-4i.
Point P is two-thirds of the horizontal distance from R to A.
For a=r=1 and b=2, y=(x-1)(x^2-2x+5); sketch a positive cubic with no stationary points and a non-stationary point of inflexion at x=1.
P and A both have coordinates (r,0).

stem_blocks.text: This question asks you to explore properties of a family of curves of the type y^2=x^3+ax+b for various values of a and b, where a and b are natural numbers.
Now, consider curves of the form y^2=x^3+b, for x>=-cuberoot(b), where b is a positive integer.
Next, consider the curve y^2=x^3+x, x>=0.
P(x,y) is defined to be a rational point on a curve if x and y are rational numbers. The tangent to y^2=x^3+ax+b at a rational point P intersects the curve at another rational point Q.
Let C be the curve y^2=x^3+2, for x>=-cuberoot(2). The rational point P(-1,-1) lies on C.

blocks.text: On the same set of axes, sketch y^2=x^3 for -2<=x<=2 and -2<=y<=2, clearly indicating any points of intersection with the coordinate axes.
On the same set of axes, sketch y^2=x^3+1 for -2<=x<=2 and -2<=y<=2, clearly indicating any points of intersection with the coordinate axes.
Write down the coordinates of the two points of inflexion on the curve y^2=x^3+1.
By considering each curve from part (a), identify two key features that would distinguish one curve from the other.
By varying the value of b, suggest two key features common to the curves y^2=x^3+b, for x>=-cuberoot(b), where b is a positive integer.
Show that dy/dx=+-(3x^2+1)/(2sqrt(x^3+x)), for x>0.
Hence deduce that the curve y^2=x^3+x has no local minimum or maximum points.

The curve y^2=x^3+x has two points of inflexion. Due to the symmetry of the curve these points have the same x-coordinate. Find this x-coordinate, giving your answer in the form x=sqrt((p sqrt(3)+q)/r), where p, q and r are integers.
Find the equation of the tangent to C at P.
Hence, find the coordinates of the rational point Q where this tangent intersects C, expressing each coordinate as a fraction.
The point S(-1,1) also lies on C. The line [QS] intersects C at a further point. Determine the coordinates of this point.

answers.text: A graph of y^2=x^3 approximately symmetric about the x-axis, with a cusp or sharp point at (0,0).
A graph of y^2=x^3+1 approximately symmetric about the x-axis, with approximately correct gradient at axes intercepts and intersections at x=-1 and y=+-1.

Valid distinguishing features include: y^2=x^3 has a cusp or sharp point while the other does not; the graphs have different domains; y^2=x^3+1 has points of inflexion; the graphs have different x- and y-intercepts.
Any two valid common features, for example: y=0 is a line of symmetry; they have one x-intercept x=-cuberoot(b); they have y-intercepts y=+-sqrt(b); they have two points of inflexion.
Local minima or maxima would require dy/dx=0, but 3x^2+1>0 for all real x, so there are no local minima or maxima.
Setting d2y/dx2=0 leads to 3x^4+6x^2-1=0. Solving for x^2 and using x>0 gives x=sqrt((2sqrt(3)-3)/3).
The tangent at P(-1,-1) is y+1=-(3/2)(x+1), equivalently y=-1.5x-2.5.
Solving the tangent with y^2=x^3+2 gives Q=(17/4,-71/8).
Line QS has slope -79/42. Solving it with y^2=x^3+2 gives the further point (127/441,-13175/9261).

classification_review.solving_path: Expands the cubic root product. Obtains coefficient expansion. Compares coefficients for p,q,r. Substitutes p and q. Expands the squared root sum. Obtains alpha^2+beta^2+gamma^2. Expands root differences. Uses preceding square-sum result. Obtains 2p^2-6q. Uses p^2<3q to make root-difference sum negative. Concludes roots cannot all be real. Compares 49 and 51. Concludes at least one complex root. Uses a valid numerical exploration. Obtains q=12. Uses cubic behavior or conjugate pairs to establish a real root. Expands four-root sum squared. Rearranges to square sum. Obtains p^2-2q. States p^2<2q. Applies 4<6 to conclude a complex root. States p^2>2q yields no conclusion. States root -1. Factors into linear and cubic factors. Obtains (x+1)(x^3-10x^2+34x-12). Uses cubic p^2=100 and 3q=102. Concludes the equation has a complex root.

stem_blocks.text: This question asks you to investigate conditions for the existence of complex roots of polynomial equations of degree 3 and 4.
The cubic equation x^3 + px^2 + qx + r = 0, where p, q, r are real, has roots alpha, beta and gamma.
Now consider polynomial equations of degree 4. The equation x^4 + px^3 + qx^2 + rx + s = 0, where p, q, r, s are real, has roots alpha, beta, gamma and delta.

For the quartic equation, in a similar way to the cubic equation, p = -(alpha + beta + gamma + delta), q = alpha beta + alpha gamma + alpha delta + beta gamma + beta delta + gamma delta, r = -(alpha beta gamma + alpha beta delta + alpha gamma delta + beta gamma delta), and s = alpha beta gamma delta.

blocks.text: By expanding (x - alpha)(x - beta)(x - gamma), show that p = -(alpha + beta + gamma), q = alpha beta + beta gamma + gamma alpha, and r = -alpha beta gamma.
Show that p^2 - 2q = alpha^2 + beta^2 + gamma^2.
Hence show that (alpha - beta)^2 + (beta - gamma)^2 + (gamma - alpha)^2 = 2p^2 - 6q.
Given that p^2 < 3q, deduce that alpha, beta and gamma cannot all be real.
Consider the equation x^3 - 7x^2 + qx + 1 = 0, where q is real. Using the result from part (c), show that when q = 17, this equation has at least one complex root.

Noah believes that if p^2 >= 3q then alpha, beta and gamma are all real. By varying the value of q in the equation x^3 - 7x^2 + qx + 1 = 0, determine the smallest positive integer value of q required to show that Noah is incorrect.
Explain why the equation will have at least one real root for all values of q.
For x^4 + px^3 + qx^2 + rx + s = 0, find an expression for alpha^2 + beta^2 + gamma^2 + delta^2 in terms of p and q.
Hence state a condition in terms of p and q that would imply x^4 + px^3 + qx^2 + rx + s = 0 has at least one complex root.
Use your result from part (f)(ii) to show that the equation x^4 - 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x + 5 = 0 has at least one complex root.
The equation x^4 - 9x^3 + 24x^2 + 22x - 12 = 0 has one integer root. State what the result in part (f)(ii) tells us when considering this equation.
Write down the integer root of this equation.
By writing x^4 - 9x^3 + 24x^2 + 22x - 12 as a product of one linear and one cubic factor, prove that the equation has at least one complex root.

answers.text: Expanding gives x^3 - (alpha + beta + gamma)x^2 + (alpha beta + beta gamma + gamma alpha)x - alpha beta gamma, so p, q and r match the stated expressions.
p^2 - 2q = (alpha + beta + gamma)^2 - 2(alpha beta + beta gamma + gamma alpha) = alpha^2 + beta^2 + gamma^2.
If p^2 < 3q, then 2p^2 - 6q < 0, so the sum of squared differences would be negative. This is impossible if all roots are real, hence they cannot all be real.
For q = 17, p = -7, so p^2 = 49 and 3q = 51. Since p^2 < 3q, the equation has at least one complex root.
A cubic curve always crosses the x-axis at least once, or complex roots of a real cubic occur in conjugate pairs so the remaining root is real.
A sufficient condition is p^2 < 2q, equivalently p^2 - 2q < 0.
For x^4 - 2x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x + 5 = 0, p = -2 and q = 3, so p^2 = 4 < 6 = 2q. Therefore there is at least one complex root.
Here p = -9 and q = 24, so p^2 = 81 > 48 = 2q; nothing can be deduced from part (f)(ii).

x^4 - 9x^3 + 24x^2 + 22x - 12 = (x + 1)(x^3 - 10x^2 + 34x - 12). For the cubic factor, p = -10 and q = 34, so p^2 = 100 < 102 = 3q; hence the cubic has at least one complex root, and therefore the original equation has at least one complex root.
